examples.problem_statement: Finding the Dilation of a Triangle. Find the image of $\triangle ABC$ in Fig. 22-26 under a dilation of $n = \frac{1}{2}$ with center of dilation at $(0,0)$.

solution.description: Read off the triangle's vertices A(1,0), B(1,1) and C(2,1) together with the dilation data: scale factor one-half and centre at the origin. Listing these first fixes exactly what the transformation will act on.

Because the centre of dilation is the origin, the image of any point is found by multiplying both of its coordinates by the scale factor one-half. This is the rule the remaining steps apply, one vertex at a time.
Halve each coordinate of A: one-half of 1 is 0.5 and one-half of 0 is 0, so A lands at (0.5, 0).
Halve each coordinate of B in the same way, sending B(1,1) to (0.5, 0.5).
Halve each coordinate of C: 2 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0.5, so C lands at (1, 0.5).

Set the three original vertices beside their three images as a check. Each side of the image triangle is half the length of the matching side of the original, which is exactly what a scale factor of one-half must produce.

examples.answer: The image is $\triangle A'B'C'$ with vertices $A'(0.5, 0)$, $B'(0.5, 0.5)$, and $C'(1, 0.5)$

examples.problem_statement:
Dilating a Square. Draw a square ABCD in the coordinate plane such that A = (1,1), B = (1,2), C = (2,1), and D = (2,2). Then,
(a) With O as the center of dilation, find the image of ABCD under a dilation with n = 1/3.
(b) Find the midpoint M of AB and the midpoint M' of A'B'.
(c) Find D_{1/3}(M).

solution.operation: For a dilation with center (0,0) and n = 1/3, we have D(x,y) = (1/3 x, 1/3 y). The image of ABCD is A'B'C'D', where A' = (1/3, 1/3), B' = (1/3, 2/3), C' = (2/3, 1/3), and D' = (2/3, 2/3).
solution.description: Apply the origin-centred rule, which divides both coordinates by 3, to all four vertices at once: A(1,1), B(1,2), C(2,1) and D(2,2) become A'(1/3,1/3), B'(1/3,2/3), C'(2/3,1/3) and D'(2/3,2/3).
Average the coordinates of A and B to get the midpoint M(1, 3/2) of the original side, then average the coordinates of A' and B' to get the midpoint M'(1/3, 1/2) of the image side.
Compare the two midpoints just computed: dilating M by the same factor of one-third produces exactly M', so this dilation carries midpoints to midpoints.

solution.description: Turn 36 degrees 24 minutes into a single decimal number of degrees: 24 minutes is 24/60 of a degree, or 0.4 degrees, so the angle is 36.4 degrees.
Part (a) asks for one quarter of the angle, so divide 36.4 degrees by 4 to get 9.1 degrees.
The 0.1 of a degree left over the 9 whole degrees is turned back into minutes by multiplying by 60, giving 6 minutes.
Report part (a) in degree-and-minute form: 9 whole degrees plus the 6 minutes just found.
Start part (b) the same way: 24 minutes is again 0.4 of a degree, so 127 degrees 24 minutes becomes 127.4 degrees.
Part (b) asks for half the angle, so divide 127.4 degrees by 2 to get 63.7 degrees.
Convert the leftover 0.7 of a degree back into minutes by multiplying by 60, giving 42 minutes.
State part (b) as 63 whole degrees and 42 minutes.
For part (c), 15 minutes is 15/60 of a degree, that is 0.25, so 81 degrees 15 minutes is 81.25 degrees.
Halve 81.25 degrees as part (c) requires, giving 40.625 degrees.
Multiply the fractional part 0.625 by 60 to get 37.5 minutes; the half minute is a further 30 seconds, so the remainder reads 37 minutes 30 seconds.
Assemble part (c) from the whole degrees and that remainder: 40 degrees, 37 minutes, 30 seconds.
Part (d) has both subunits, so convert each: 29 minutes is 29/60 of a degree and 20 seconds is 20/3600 of a degree, giving about 74.4889 degrees.
Take one quarter of 74.4889 degrees, about 18.6222 degrees, as part (d) asks.
Multiply the leftover 0.6222 of a degree by 60 to get about 37.333 minutes; the 0.333 of a minute is 20 seconds, so the remainder is 37 minutes 20 seconds.
Assemble part (d) from the whole degrees and that remainder: 18 degrees, 37 minutes, 20 seconds.

concept.technique_name: trigonometric functions from a point on the terminal side

examples.problem_statement: Determine the values of the trigonometric functions of angle θ (smallest positive angle in standard position) if P is a point on the terminal side of θ and the coordinates of P are (a) P(3, 4), (b) P(−3,4), (c) P(−1,−3). See Fig. 24-7.

solution.description: Write down the six ratios in terms of the coordinates x and y of a point on the terminal side and its distance r from the origin. Every part that follows is just these definitions with numbers substituted.
For P(3,4) the distance from the origin is the square root of 3 squared plus 4 squared, that is the square root of 25, so r equals 5.
Substitute x = 3, y = 4 and r = 5 into the six definitions. P lies in the first quadrant, where both coordinates are positive, so all six ratios come out positive.
For P(-3,4) the squares of the coordinates are again 9 and 16, so r is again 5. Squaring removes the sign, and a distance is never negative.
Substitute x = -3, y = 4 and r = 5. Only x is negative, so sine and cosecant stay positive while cosine, secant, tangent and cotangent all turn negative, as expected in the second quadrant.
For P(-1,-3) the sum of the squares is 1 plus 9, so r is the square root of 10, which does not simplify to a whole number.

Substitute x = -1, y = -3 and r = root 10. Both coordinates are negative, so sine and cosine are negative, while tangent and cotangent, each a ratio of two negatives, are positive. The surds are then rationalized to give the standard forms.

examples.answer: Verified: (a) sinθ=4/5, cosθ=3/5, tanθ=4/3, cotθ=3/4, secθ=5/3, cscθ=5/4; (b) sinθ=4/5, cosθ=−3/5, tanθ=−4/3, cotθ=−3/4, secθ=−5/3, cscθ=5/4; (c) sinθ=−3√10/10, cosθ=−√10/10, tanθ=3, cotθ=1/3, secθ=−√10, cscθ=−√10/3

examples.problem_statement: Find the possible values of sin θ and tan θ, given cos θ = 5/6.

solution.operation: Since cos θ = x/r = 5/6, take x = 5, r = 6. Compute y = ±√(r² - x²) = ±√(36 - 25) = ±√11.
solution.description: Read cos theta = 5/6 as x over r, so take x = 5 and r = 6. The Pythagorean relation then gives y as plus or minus the square root of 36 minus 25, that is plus or minus root 11; no quadrant was stated, so both signs must be carried forward.

solution.operation: Case (a): θ in quadrant I → y = √11. Then sin θ = y/r = √11/6, tan θ = y/x = √11/5.
solution.description: Take the positive root first. With x and y both positive the angle lies in quadrant I, and dividing y by r gives sin theta = root 11 over 6, while dividing y by x gives tan theta = root 11 over 5.

solution.operation: Case (b): θ in quadrant IV → y = -√11. Then sin θ = y/r = -√11/6, tan θ = y/x = -√11/5.
solution.description: Now take the negative root. With x positive and y negative the angle lies in quadrant IV, so the same two divisions give sin theta = minus root 11 over 6 and tan theta = minus root 11 over 5.

examples.problem_statement: Find the possible values of sin θ and cos θ, given tan θ = -3/4.

solution.description: Record the given ratio, tangent of theta equals negative three quarters. Tangent is sine divided by cosine, so this one number constrains the pair of values we are looking for.

A negative tangent means sine and cosine carry opposite signs, which happens only in quadrant II, where sine is positive and cosine negative, or quadrant IV, where the signs are reversed. Both cases have to be followed to the end.
Bring in the identity that sine squared plus cosine squared equals one; it will pin down the actual sizes once the ratio between them is known.

solution.operation: Express sine in terms of cosine
solution.description: Rewrite the given ratio as sine equals negative three quarters of cosine, so the identity can be expressed in cosine alone.
Substitute that expression for sine into the identity, leaving a single equation whose only unknown is cosine.
Square the coefficient: negative three quarters squared is nine sixteenths, so the equation becomes nine sixteenths of cosine squared plus cosine squared equals one.
Add the two cosine-squared terms, nine sixteenths plus sixteen sixteenths, to get twenty-five sixteenths of cosine squared equals one.
Multiply both sides by sixteen twenty-fifths to isolate cosine squared, which equals sixteen twenty-fifths.
Take the square root of both sides. Both signs are still admissible here, so cosine is plus or minus four fifths, one value for each of the two quadrants identified earlier.
Feed each cosine value back through the relation from step 4 to obtain the sine that accompanies it.
The negative cosine, minus four fifths, is the quadrant II case; negative three quarters times minus four fifths gives sine equal to three fifths, positive as quadrant II requires.
The positive cosine, four fifths, is the quadrant IV case; negative three quarters times four fifths gives sine equal to minus three fifths, negative as quadrant IV requires.

examples.answer: In quadrant II: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = -4/5; in quadrant IV: sin θ = -3/5, cos θ = 4/5.

examples.problem_statement: Find the values of the remaining functions of θ, given sin θ = √3/2 and cos θ = -1/2.

solution.operation: Determine quadrant: since sin θ > 0 and cos θ < 0, θ is in quadrant II.
solution.description: A positive sine together with a negative cosine can only occur in quadrant II, so the signs of the coordinates are settled before any computation begins.

solution.operation: Assign coordinates: x = -1, y = √3, then compute r = √[(-1)² + (√3)²] = √(1+3) = 2.
solution.description: Choose coordinates that match the given ratios: x = -1 and y = root 3. The distance r is then the square root of 1 plus 3, that is 2, which reproduces sin theta = root 3 over 2 and cos theta = minus one half.
Divide y by x to get the tangent: root 3 over negative one, that is negative root 3, negative as quadrant II demands.
Secant is the reciprocal of the given cosine, so one divided by minus one half gives negative 2.
Cotangent is the reciprocal of the tangent just found; one over negative root 3 rationalizes to minus root 3 over 3.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of the given sine; two over root 3 rationalizes to two root 3 over 3.

examples.answer: tan θ = -√3, cot θ = -√3/3, sec θ = -2, csc θ = 2√3/3

examples.problem_statement: Determine the possible values of cos θ and tan θ if sin θ = m/n, a negative fraction.

solution.operation: Since sin θ is negative, θ is in quadrant III or IV.
solution.description: A negative sine means y is negative while r stays positive, so the terminal side falls in quadrant III or quadrant IV. Both cases must be worked out.

solution.operation: In quadrant III: take y = m (negative), r = n, then x = -√(n² - m²).
solution.description: For the quadrant III case set y = m, which is negative, and r = n. There x is negative too, so x is minus the square root of n squared minus m squared.

solution.operation: Compute cos θ = x/r = -√(n² - m²)/n and tan θ = y/x = m / (-√(n² - m²)) = -m/√(n² - m²).
solution.description: Divide to get the two required functions in quadrant III: cosine is that negative x over n, and tangent is m over the negative x, which simplifies to minus m over the root.

solution.operation: In quadrant IV: take y = m (negative), r = n, then x = +√(n² - m²).
solution.description: For the quadrant IV case keep y = m and r = n, but now x is positive, so x is plus the square root of n squared minus m squared.

solution.operation: Compute cos θ = x/r = √(n² - m²)/n and tan θ = y/x = m / √(n² - m²).
solution.description: The same two divisions with the positive x give cosine as the root over n and tangent as m over the root, a positive cosine paired with a negative tangent, as quadrant IV requires.

examples.answer: In quadrant III: cos θ = -√(n² - m²)/n, tan θ = -m/√(n² - m²); in quadrant IV: cos θ = √(n² - m²)/n, tan θ = m/√(n² - m²)

examples.problem_statement: Find the values of the trigonometric functions of the acute angles of the right triangle ABC given b = 24 and c = 25.

solution.operation: Identify given values and right triangle properties
solution.description: Set up the triangle: the right angle sits at C, so c = 25 is the hypotenuse and b = 24 is the leg adjacent to angle A. The third side, leg a, is still unknown.

solution.operation: Find the missing side using Pythagorean theorem
solution.description: Recover the missing leg from a squared equals c squared minus b squared, that is 625 minus 576, or 49, so a = 7 and this is the 7-24-25 right triangle.

solution.operation: Define trigonometric ratios for angle A
solution.description: For angle A the opposite leg is a = 7 and the adjacent leg is b = 24, so sine is 7/25, cosine is 24/25 and tangent is 7/24.

solution.operation: Find reciprocal trigonometric ratios for angle A
solution.result: \begin{aligned}\csc A = \frac{1}{\sin A} = \frac{25}{7} \\ \sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{25}{24} \\ \cot A = \frac{1}{\tan A} = \frac{24}{7}\end{aligned}
solution.description: Invert those three ratios to get the reciprocal functions of A: cosecant 25/7, secant 25/24 and cotangent 24/7.

solution.operation: Define trigonometric ratios for angle B
solution.description: For angle B the two legs change roles: b = 24 is now the opposite side and a = 7 the adjacent one, giving sine 24/25, cosine 7/25 and tangent 24/7.

solution.operation: Find reciprocal trigonometric ratios for angle B
solution.result: \begin{aligned}\csc B = \frac{1}{\sin B} = \frac{25}{24} \\ \sec B = \frac{1}{\cos B} = \frac{25}{7} \\ \cot B = \frac{1}{\tan B} = \frac{7}{24}\end{aligned}
solution.description: Invert the three ratios of B in the same way to get cosecant 25/24, secant 25/7 and cotangent 7/24.

solution.result: \begin{aligned}\sin A = \cos B = \frac{7}{25} \\ \cos A = \sin B = \frac{24}{25} \\ \tan A = \cot B = \frac{7}{24}\end{aligned}
solution.description: Check the work against the co-function relations: A and B are complementary, so sine of A must equal cosine of B, cosine of A must equal sine of B and tangent of A must equal cotangent of B. All three hold for the values computed.

examples.answer: Verified correct: For angle A: sin A = 7/25, cos A = 24/25, tan A = 7/24, cot A = 24/7, sec A = 25/24, csc A = 25/7. For angle B: sin B = 24/25, cos B = 7/25, tan B = 24/7, cot B = 7/24, sec B = 25/7, csc B = 25/24.

examples.problem_statement: Find the values of the trigonometric functions of the acute angles of the right triangle ABC, given a = 2, c = 2√5.

solution.operation: Compute b using Pythagorean theorem: b² = c² - a² = (2√5)² - 2² = 20 - 4 = 16 → b = 4
solution.description: Repeat the Pythagorean step on the new triangle: b squared equals c squared minus a squared, that is 20 minus 4, or 16, so the missing leg is b = 4.

solution.operation: Simplify ratios for angle A: sin A = 2/(2√5) = √5/5, cos A = 4/(2√5) = 2√5/5, tan A = 2/4 = 1/2, etc.
solution.description: Form the ratios for angle A from opposite 2, adjacent 4 and hypotenuse 2 root 5, then clear the surd from each denominator: sine becomes root 5 over 5, cosine becomes 2 root 5 over 5 and tangent reduces to one half.

solution.operation: Observe co-function identities: sin A = cos B, cos A = sin B, tan A = cot B, etc.
solution.description: Rather than recomputing everything for angle B, use the co-function relations between the complementary angles: sine and cosine swap, tangent and cotangent swap, so the six values for B are read straight off those for A.

examples.answer: For angle A: sin A = √5/5, cos A = 2√5/5, tan A = 1/2, cot A = 2, sec A = √5/2, csc A = √5. For angle B: sin B = 2√5/5, cos B = √5/5, tan B = 2, cot B = 1/2, sec B = √5, csc B = √5/2.

examples.problem_statement: Find the values of the trigonometric functions of the acute angle A, given sin A = 3/7.

solution.description: We are given that the sine of angle A is 3/7. In a right triangle, sine is defined as opposite/hypotenuse.
Since sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = 3/7, we can assign these values to the sides of a right triangle with angle A.

concept.technique_name: trigonometric functions of an acute angle

examples.problem_statement: If A is acute and tan A = x/1, determine the values of the remaining functions.

solution.description: Read the given ratio as a shape: tangent is opposite over adjacent, so build a right triangle whose leg opposite A has length x and whose adjacent leg has length 1. Because A is acute, x is positive and this triangle exists.
With legs x and 1, the Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse as the square root of x squared plus one.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so divide the leg x by the hypotenuse just found.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so divide the leg 1 by that same hypotenuse.
Tangent needs no computation: it is the ratio the problem supplied, x over 1, which is simply x.
Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, so it is one over x. This requires x to be nonzero, which holds since A is acute.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine; inverting one over the root leaves the root of x squared plus one.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine; inverting x over the root gives the root of x squared plus one, divided by x.

examples.answer: sin A = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}, cos A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}, tan A = x, cot A = \frac{1}{x}, sec A = \sqrt{x^2 + 1}, csc A = \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{x}

examples.problem_statement: Find the value of the trigonometric functions of 45°.

solution.operation: Consider an isosceles right triangle ABC where angles A and B are both 45°, so sides a and b are equal.
solution.description: The two acute angles of a 45 degree right triangle are equal, so the legs opposite them are equal; an isosceles right triangle is therefore the figure to use.
Only the ratios of the sides matter here, so choose the simplest convenient legs and set both equal to 1.
The hypotenuse follows from the Pythagorean theorem: the square root of 1 plus 1, that is root 2.
Sine of 45 degrees is the opposite leg 1 over the hypotenuse root 2; rationalizing the denominator gives one half of root 2.
Cosine of 45 degrees uses the adjacent leg, which is also 1, over the same hypotenuse, so it comes out equal to the sine.
Tangent of 45 degrees is one leg over the other, 1 over 1, which is exactly 1.
Cotangent is the reciprocal of that tangent, so for 45 degrees it is also 1.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine; inverting 1 over root 2 gives root 2.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, which at 45 degrees equals the cosine, so it is root 2 as well.

examples.answer: sin 45° = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}, cos 45° = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}, tan 45° = 1, cot 45° = 1, sec 45° = \sqrt{2}, csc 45° = \sqrt{2}

common_mistakes: Copying the given tangent instead of inverting it, and writing cot A = x rather than 1 over x.
Taking the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs x and 1 to be x + 1 instead of the square root of x squared plus one.
